prediction:
THOUGHT: The patient is a 50-year-old woman presenting with flaccid, non-pruritic blisters on the forearm (10% TBSA), positive Nikolsky sign (indicating epidermal detachment with minimal pressure), and painful mucosal ulcers involving oral (buccal, gingival) and genital (vulvar) surfaces. This widespread mucocutaneous blistering strongly suggests an autoimmune blistering disease. The skin biopsy shows acantholysis and intraepidermal blister formation — hallmark features of pemphigus (as opposed to subepidermal blistering seen in bullous pemphigoid or epidermolysis bullosa acquisita). Direct immunofluorescence reveals intercellular IgG and C3 deposition in the epidermis — the classic finding in pemphigus vulgaris (PV), reflecting autoantibodies targeting desmosomal adhesion proteins (primarily desmoglein 3, and often desmoglein 1 in mucocutaneous cases). Serum testing confirms desmoglein antibodies, further supporting this. While drug-induced pemphigus is rare, captopril (an ACE inhibitor) is a well-documented trigger of pemphigus vulgaris — especially mucocutaneous forms — and the timing (recent initiation) fits. Meloxicam discontinuation 2 weeks prior is less likely causative, as NSAIDs are not associated with pemphigus. The absence of systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy) and normal CBC argue against paraneoplastic pemphigus or lymphoproliferative disorders. Pernicious anemia and Graves’ disease in the family suggest an underlying autoimmune diathesis, increasing susceptibility. Other considerations — such as bullous pemphigoid (typically elderly, tense blisters, subepidermal histology, linear IgG/C3 at basement membrane), erythema multiforme (target lesions, history of HSV, acute onset, self-limited), or Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (fever, systemic illness, extensive epidermal detachment, negative DIF for intercellular IgG) — are inconsistent with the clinical and lab findings.

DIAGNOSIS: Pemphigus vulgaris
